strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem of fragmented EEG-FM evaluation protocols with a comprehensive, well-designed benchmark integrating 14 datasets across 10 paradigms
Rigorous experimental methodology with multiple fine-tuning strategies, task setups, and classifier configurations, proper statistical reporting across 5 seeds
Diagnostic analyses beyond performance metrics using gradient similarity, subspace affinity, CKA, and RSA provide valuable interpretability into model behavior

Identifies several practical insights including multi-task learning as regularization, gradient conflicts between reconstruction and classification objectives, and compact models with inductive biases outperforming large models
Well-documented with detailed experimental settings, standardized preprocessing pipeline, and promised code release supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Primarily a benchmarking contribution without proposing methods to address identified problems; gradient conflicts are diagnosed but no solutions demonstrated or validated

Gradient conflict analysis uses aggressive dimensionality reduction (6D via CountSketch) without sensitivity analysis or justification; interpretation of near-zero correlations lacks depth regarding causality and practical remedies
Key findings are somewhat expected in modern deep learning context (frozen models don't transfer well, multi-task learning helps, inductive biases matter); lacks surprising mechanistic insights

Critical phenomena under-explored: CSBrain collapse briefly mentioned in appendix deserves investigation; multi-task negative transfer mentioned but not analyzed; scaling law deviation based on only 9 models with confounded architectural differences

Design fairness concerns: Model-specific adaptations (dynamic routing for BENDR/BIOT, channel reordering for CSBrain) may bias comparisons; unclear if they systematically disadvantage certain architectures
Scope creep dilutes impact by covering multiple topics (scaling laws, multi-task learning, architectural inductive biases, gradient dynamics) without deep investigation of any single aspect
Presentation issues: Difficult-to-interpret radar charts; small heatmaps; key findings buried in appendix; overwhelming main paper plus 35-page appendix structure
Missing comparisons: No statistical significance testing between models; no baselines with non-pretrained approaches or traditional signal processing; limited cross-domain validation of insights

strengths: Addresses genuine need for standardized EEG-FM evaluation with fragmented protocols currently hindering fair comparison
Comprehensive empirical study spanning 14 datasets, 9 models, multiple fine-tuning strategies and experimental configurations with appropriate statistical reporting (5 seeds, class-imbalance metrics)
Systematic diagnostic analysis beyond end-task metrics using gradient analysis (cosine similarity, subspace affinity, conflict detection) and representation similarity tools (CKA, RSA)
Well-engineered reproducible framework with standardized preprocessing pipeline, modular open-source architecture, and detailed experimental documentation
Clear actionable recommendations for future EEG-FM development regarding multi-task learning, gradient alignment, and architectural design priorities
weaknesses: Limited novelty for ICML—purely empirical benchmarking contribution with no methodological innovations; findings (multi-task regularization, scaling law deviations, gradient conflicts) largely validate predictable transfer learning principles rather than reveal surprising insights

Key findings lack mechanistic depth: gradient conflict analysis identifies the problem but proposes no solutions; scaling analysis is descriptive rather than explanatory, with unexplored alternative hypotheses about hyperparameter fairness and data heterogeneity

Significant experimental design concerns: heterogeneous model adaptations (dynamic routing blocks for some models, just channel removal for others) could introduce systematic bias; fairness of forcing unified fine-tuning on models designed for different paradigms (e.g., EEGPT for frozen backbone)

Weak analysis of multi-task learning claims: oversimplified narrative despite acknowledged negative transfer cases; uniform resampling is naive when established conflict resolution methods (PCGrad, task weighting) exist but remain unexplored

Statistical rigor below conference standards: no significance testing between model pairs, only 5 random seeds (insufficient for tiny datasets like TUSL with 290 samples), missing confidence intervals and ablation studies isolating individual mechanism contributions

Limited scope and generalizability: all findings specific to EEG domain with unclear transfer to other modalities or general transfer learning principles; incomplete paradigm coverage (1-2 datasets per paradigm, missing multimodal settings); rapid model evolution makes benchmark temporally fragile

Presentation issues: overcrowded paper attempting too many analyses; unreadable heatmaps (Figures 3-4); critical limitations relegated to Appendix F.1; incomplete code link; unclear practical guidance (e.g., when to use single vs. multi-task given negative transfer can occur)

strengths: Addresses a real and important gap: the fragmented evaluation landscape for EEG foundation models needed standardization
Comprehensive benchmark design: 14 diverse datasets, systematic configuration space (3 fine-tuning strategies × 2 task setups × 3 classifier heads), careful preprocessing standardization

Sophisticated diagnostic tools: gradient-space analysis (cosine similarity, subspace affinity, conflict detection) and representation-space analysis (CKA, RSA) provide mechanistic insights beyond accuracy metrics
Reproducible and rigorous: multiple random seeds, detailed experimental setup, promised open-source code, standard datasets with clear split procedures
Striking empirical finding: compact models (CBraMod: 4.92M params) outperform much larger models (REVE: 69.19M params) despite superior pre-training data, challenging conventional scaling narratives
Extensive empirical evaluation: 7 EEG-specific + 2 general time-series models across comprehensive tables and visualizations
Layer-wise analysis reveals that pre-training stabilizes Transformer backbones while shifting optimization burden to input embeddings
weaknesses: Limited mechanistic explanation of key findings: why compact models outperform larger ones remains observational rather than explained; gradient conflicts are identified but not solved; recommendations are vague ('rethink objectives')

Experimental design concerns: different models required different adaptations (dynamic-routing blocks, channel flattening, adapters) raising fairness questions; unclear if hyperparameter tuning effort was equal across models

Somewhat expected/incremental findings: frozen backbone failure is expected when distributions differ; multi-task learning as regularizer is well-established in ML; simple classifier heads working best on noisy data is intuitive
Incomplete solutions: identified problems (gradient conflicts, negative transfer in multi-task learning) are diagnosed but not addressed with proposed solutions
Limited statistical rigor: no formal significance testing or correction for multiple comparisons; large variance in some results makes interpretation difficult
Limited scope: all models are transformer-based; no comparison with classical methods (CSP, Riemannian geometry); dramatic variation in dataset sizes (290 to 500K samples) with unclear generalization
Missing ablations: no study of preprocessing steps, montage variation effects, or how findings depend on dataset size regimes
Incomplete scaling analysis: Figure 1 lacks dimensionality decomposition (architecture type, depth, width separately); pre-training data quality not analyzed separate from quantity
Critical details relegated to appendix: model-specific adaptations (Section B.6) are crucial for fair comparison but appear late in supplementary material

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous benchmark design integrating 14 datasets, 10 paradigms, 9 models with multiple evaluation dimensions (3 fine-tuning strategies, 2 task setups, 3 classifier heads)
Methodologically sound with appropriate handling of class imbalance, overlap-sensitive datasets explicitly marked, results across 5 random seeds with standard deviations
Novel diagnostic insights into transfer learning bottlenecks, particularly gradient conflict analysis between reconstruction and classification objectives revealing weak alignment (Figure 8)
Provides actionable empirical guidance (multi-task as regularizer but risk of negative transfer; capacity-stability tradeoffs in classifiers; EEG-specific design importance)
Excellent reproducibility: standardized preprocessing, public datasets, promised code release, detailed appendices, honest limitations discussion
Addresses real problem of fragmented EEG-FM evaluation that impedes fair comparison and scientific progress
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (gradient analysis, CKA, RSA, subspace affinity) to EEG domain without novel analytical methods

Gradient conflict analysis has technical issues: comparing MSE and Cross-Entropy losses at different scales is inherently problematic; CountSketch projection (d=1024) lacks justification; no per-layer analysis to identify conflict severity
Confounding model-specific adaptations (dynamic routing, adapters, channel flattening) complicate fair comparison and mask architectural contributions
No statistical significance testing of performance differences despite reporting means/std devs; lacks confidence intervals on reported correlations

Multi-task learning analysis limited: simple resampling for imbalance; negative transfer identified but not deeply analyzed for task combinations; shared optimizer acknowledged as suboptimal but not addressed
Scale analysis incomplete: only examines released checkpoints under specific protocol; data volume estimation crude; doesn't systematically explore scaling laws
Unclear generalization beyond matched protocol and released checkpoints; no cross-dataset generalization or domain shift analysis
Representational convergence findings (Figure 7) show alignment in scratch setting too, weakening claims about pre-training benefits

strengths: Addresses a genuine need in the EEG-FM community for standardized evaluation protocols
Comprehensive scope: 14 datasets, 9 models, multiple fine-tuning strategies and classifier designs with extensive experiments
Diagnostic tools beyond performance metrics (gradient analysis, CKA/RSA, visualization)
Detailed reproducibility: standardized preprocessing, open-source promise, 5-seed reporting
Some interesting observations about gradient conflicts and multi-task learning effects
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily benchmarking infrastructure without new methodology or significant algorithmic contributions
Lack of actionable insights: identifies problems (gradient conflicts, negative transfer) but provides no solutions or guidance; vague future directions
Methodology undermined by model-specific adapters and per-model preprocessing that contradict the 'unified protocol' claim
Data leakage: pre-training/evaluation overlap (LaBraM-SEED, EEGPT-SEED/PhysioMI) despite being marked and excluded
Shallow analysis: gradient/representation analysis is descriptive rather than explanatory; no investigation of why findings occur
No demonstrated impact: paper identifies issues but doesn't propose, test, or validate improvements; unclear if benchmark adoption will occur
Overstated claims: 'scale doesn't explain transfer' understates Figure 1's evident correlation; weak evidence for strong conclusions
Scope creep: attempts benchmarking, diagnostics, visualization without sufficient depth; more like technical report than research contribution
Limited generalization: classification-only tasks, public datasets only, no clinical validation or real-world deployment investigation
Missing actionable framework: no algorithm for task grouping, gradient conflict resolution, or predicting which approach works when

strengths: Addresses a critical and acknowledged need: standardized evaluation of EEG-FMs solves genuine fragmentation problem in the field
Rigorous experimental design: 14 datasets × 10 paradigms × 7 models × multiple fine-tuning strategies with careful attention to reproducibility and fairness
Sophisticated diagnostic analyses: integration of gradient and representation analysis (CKA, RSA, subspace affinity) provides mechanistic understanding beyond performance metrics
Transparent methodology: explicit handling of model-specific adaptations, overlap-sensitive cases, and protocol-conditional comparisons; honest limitations discussion
High reproducibility: standardized preprocessing, multiple random seeds, promised open-source codebase, comprehensive implementation details
Actionable insights: identified findings (frozen-backbone gaps, gradient conflicts, multi-task regularization, architectural importance) have immediate practical value
Well-presented and comprehensive: clear organization, informative figures, extensive appendices with detailed results and supplementary analysis
Likely to become community standard: infrastructure contribution will enable fairer comparisons and reproducible science in EEG-FM research
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a benchmark/empirical study applying standard analysis techniques (CKA, RSA, gradient analysis) rather than proposing new methods or theoretical frameworks

Partially expected findings: larger models/more data help (unsurprising); frozen representations from reconstruction pre-training don't transfer well (expected); multi-task as regularizer (known); most novel insight (gradient conflicts) lacks deep mechanistic explanation

Insufficient actionable guidance for future work: recommendations remain generic ('better pre-training objectives,' 'EEG-specific design') without concrete proposals for addressing identified bottlenecks

Model comparison confounds: REVE's significantly larger pre-training corpus (25,000 vs. thousands of subjects) complicates 'which model is better' comparisons; treated as empirical finding rather than confound
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: why negative transfer occurs in specific paradigms unexplained; gradient conflicts identified but solutions not proposed; frozen-backbone gap not deeply analyzed
Multi-task learning analysis limitations: resampling for dataset balance could introduce systematic biases; task incompatibility identified but not mechanistically understood
Technical justifications could be stronger: rank-6 PCA choice insufficiently justified; CountSketch dimension (1024) appears arbitrary; sensitivity analyses would strengthen claims
Scope limitations (appropriately acknowledged): classification-only focus; no multi-modal, closed-source, or advanced clinical applications; domain-specific work primarily beneficial to EEG community
